title: ReadyToRun and Native AOT
description: Compare ReadyToRun and Native AOT compilation strategies, understand their trade-offs, and learn when to use each.

data.text: Traditional .NET applications rely on the JIT compiler to produce native code at runtime. This gives you flexibility — the same assembly runs on x64, ARM64, and Linux without recompilation — but it also means every cold start includes JIT work. ReadyToRun and Native AOT are two different strategies for moving that compilation work out of the critical startup path and into the build pipeline.

ReadyToRun produces a partially compiled application. Native AOT produces a fully compiled, self-contained executable with no runtime dependency. Choosing between them is not about which is objectively better — it is about which trade-off your application can tolerate. Serverless functions, containerized microservices, and CLI tools each have different constraints.

When you publish with ReadyToRun, the .NET SDK produces a native image for your target architecture. This image contains precompiled versions of the methods in your assemblies. At startup, the runtime loads these images directly instead of JIT-compiling from CIL. The startup is faster, especially for large applications with many assemblies. However, the runtime still needs the .NET runtime libraries, and some methods — like generics instantiated with new types at runtime — will still be JIT-compiled on demand.

items: Produces a `.dll` or `.exe` alongside a `.ni.dll` native image.
Requires the .NET runtime to be present on the target machine (framework-dependent) or shipped (self-contained).
Reduces JIT time by 30-70% for typical web applications.
Does not eliminate the runtime entirely — GC, reflection, and dynamic code generation still work.
Publish size increases by roughly 10-20% due to the native images.

data.title: Publishing ReadyToRun images
data.code:
# Self-contained publish with ReadyToRun for Linux ARM64
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-arm64 \
  -p:PublishReadyToRun=true \
  -p:PublishSingleFile=false \
  --self-contained true

# Inspect the ReadyToRun header of an assembly
dotnet dump analyze --type r2r <path-to-app.dll>

data.text: Native AOT: fully native, no runtime

Native AOT takes compilation further. It compiles your entire application — including the runtime libraries it uses — into a single native executable. The resulting binary starts in milliseconds, uses less memory at rest, and does not require the .NET runtime to be installed separately. The trade-off is significant: compilation times are much longer, publish sizes are larger, and some runtime features like reflection and `dynamic` are heavily restricted or require pre-configuration.

items: Produces a single native executable file with no runtime dependency.
Startup times measured in milliseconds — ideal for serverless and CLI tools.
Smaller memory footprint because the runtime is stripped to only what is used.
Reflection and `dynamic` are limited by trimming; you must configure supported types explicitly.
Generic types must be known at compile time or pre-registered.

data.text: Choosing between ReadyToRun and Native AOT

items.title: ReadyToRun
items.description: Best for server applications, containers, and long-running services where startup improvement matters but runtime flexibility is needed. Faster publish, broader API compatibility, still requires .NET runtime.

items.title: Native AOT
items.description: Best for serverless functions, CLI tools, edge deployments, and environments where you cannot install a runtime. Ultra-fast startup, minimal deployment footprint, but requires trimming configuration and loses some runtime features.

data.title: Trimming is the hidden cost of AOT
data.text: Both ReadyToRun and Native AOT enable the ILLinker tree-shaker by default in Release builds. The linker removes unused code to reduce size. If your application uses reflection — especially common in ASP.NET Core minimal APIs or serialization libraries — the linker may remove types your application needs at runtime. You must configure `rd.xml` or use the `DynamicDependency` attribute to preserve those types. Test your AOT builds thoroughly with reflection-heavy code paths.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: ReadyToRun precompiles to native images at build time and requires the .NET runtime at deployment.
Native AOT produces a fully standalone native executable with no runtime dependency.
Both technologies use the ILLinker for tree-shaking; reflection-heavy code needs explicit preservation.
Choose ReadyToRun for services and containers; choose Native AOT for serverless, CLI, and edge scenarios.
